newsitem.title: UK: Storm over all-male crew for Cabot memorial voyage.
newsitem.headline: Storm over all-male crew for Cabot memorial voyage.

text.p: A veteran yachtsman ran into a storm on Thursday when he named an all-male crew for a project to re-enact the 15th-century discovery of Newfoundland.
Two prominent British women sailors denounced the decision of David Alan-Williams to take 19 fellow men on the gruelling voyage as sex discrimination.

Alan-Williams is planning to leave the western English port of Bristol on May 2 in a 40-tonne bunkless craft modelled on the one in which explorer John Cabot set out on his transatlantic odyssey exactly 500 years previously.
He had 10 applications from women to be crew members, and about nine times that number from men.

"The women had the enthusiasm and skill, but they could not meet the strength factor. This is a tough voyage in a tiny vessel and requires physical strength," he said after announcing his crew at a London boat show.

But Samantha Brewster, the first woman to sail single-handedly around the world from east to west against prevailing winds, rejected his reasoning, saying teamwork was more important on such a voyage than brute strength.
"This is just an excuse for being sexist," she said.
Another round-the-world yachtswoman, Lisa Clayton, added: "It seems so old-fashioned and a bit sad. I would have thought on a 20-strong crew there would be room for both sexes."
Cabot, a Venetian whose real name was Giovanni Caboto, sailed from Bristol in 1497 with an all-male crew.
His appeal for funds for a voyage had been rejected by Spain and Portugal but won support from England's Henry VII.
Historians say Henry's backing may have been the factor which determined that North America was colonised by English rather than Iberian peoples.
Cabot took 52 days to reach Newfoundland. On the way, he discovered the world's richest fishing grounds off the Grand Banks.
